options.B: Petrol engines are limited by abnormal pre-ignition and knocking (auto-ignition of end gas), whereas diesel engines compress only pure air and rely on high compression temperature to self-ignite injected diesel fuel
options.C: Diesel engines have lighter pistons and thinner cylinder walls
options.D: High compression ratios lower the thermal efficiency of petrol engines

explanation: In SI (petrol) engines, a homogeneous air-fuel mixture is compressed. If compression ratio exceeds approx 10:1 to 12:1, compression heat causes the unburned end-gas to auto-ignite spontaneously before the flame front arrives, producing violent pressure waves known as knocking or detonation. In CI (diesel) engines, only air is compressed, eliminating knock during compression; the air temperature must exceed the auto-ignition point of diesel (approx 500 deg C) to ensure self-ignition upon fuel injection.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a typical crankcase-scavenged two-stroke petrol engine, what is the opening and closing sequence of the cylinder ports during the downward power stroke?

options.A: Transfer port opens first, then Exhaust port opens
options.B: Exhaust port opens first (blowdown), followed shortly by the Transfer port opening
options.C: Inlet port opens first, then Transfer port opens
options.D: All three ports open simultaneously at Bottom Dead Center (BDC)

explanation: As the piston moves downward on the expansion/power stroke: (1) The upper piston edge first uncovers the Exhaust Port (approx 50 to 60 degrees before BDC). High-pressure exhaust gases rapidly discharge into the atmosphere (exhaust blowdown), dropping cylinder pressure below crankcase pressure; (2) The piston then uncovers the Transfer Port (approx 35 to 45 degrees before BDC), allowing pre-compressed fresh charge from the crankcase to enter and scavenge the cylinder.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the formula for calculating Indicated Power (IP) in kilowatts (kW) of a multi-cylinder four-stroke engine having mean effective pressure P_mi (bar), stroke length L (m), piston area A (m^2), engine speed N (rpm), and k cylinders?

options.B: IP = (P_mi * L * A * N * k) / 60

explanation: Indicated power is the rate of work done on the piston crowns by the expanding combustion gases: IP = (P_mi * L * A * n * k) / 60 kW, where P_mi is mean effective pressure in kPa (1 bar = 100 kPa), and n is the number of power strokes per minute. For a 4-stroke engine, n = N / 2; for a 2-stroke engine, n = N. Therefore, for a 4-stroke engine with P_mi in bar: IP = (P_mi * 100 * L * A * (N/2) * k) / 60 kW. Brake power measured at the dynamometer shaft is BP = (2 * pi * N * T) / 60 kW.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How does the Mechanical Efficiency (eta_m = BP / IP) of an internal combustion engine behave as engine load increases from zero (idling) to full rated load at constant rotational speed?

options.A: Decreases continuously to zero at full load
options.B: Increases continuously from zero at no load to its maximum value at full load
options.C: Remains perfectly constant across all load conditions
options.D: Reaches 100% at half load and decreases thereafter

explanation: Mechanical efficiency is eta_m = BP / IP = BP / (BP + FP). At constant speed, engine frictional power (FP) is predominantly governed by piston ring sliding friction, bearing friction, and pumping work, which remain nearly constant regardless of load. At no-load (idling), useful Brake Power is zero (BP = 0), so eta_m = 0. As load increases, BP increases while FP remains nearly constant, causing the ratio BP / (BP + FP) to rise steadily to its peak value (typically 80-90%) at full rated load.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the relationship between Brake Thermal Efficiency (eta_bt), Indicated Thermal Efficiency (eta_it), and Mechanical Efficiency (eta_m)?

options.A: eta_bt = eta_it / eta_m
options.B: eta_bt = eta_m * eta_it
options.C: eta_bt = eta_it + eta_m

explanation: Indicated thermal efficiency is eta_it = IP / (m_dot_f * CV) and Brake thermal efficiency is eta_bt = BP / (m_dot_f * CV), where m_dot_f is fuel mass flow rate (kg/s) and CV is calorific value (kJ/kg). Since mechanical efficiency is eta_m = BP / IP, we have: eta_bt = (BP / IP) * [IP / (m_dot_f * CV)] = eta_m * eta_it. Brake thermal efficiency represents the net fraction of fuel chemical energy converted into shaft work.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is 'Brake Specific Fuel Consumption' (BSFC), and why is it preferred over total fuel consumption for comparing the fuel economy of different engines?

options.A: It is fuel consumption per unit cylinder volume, independent of engine speed
options.B: It is the mass of fuel consumed per unit brake power output per unit time (BSFC = m_dot_f / BP in kg/kW-h), normalizing fuel consumption against power delivered
options.C: It is the ratio of air mass to fuel mass in the exhaust gas
options.D: It is the volume of fuel required to overcome frictional power at idle

explanation: A large 500 kW diesel engine naturally consumes more total fuel per hour than a small 20 kW engine. Total fuel consumption alone cannot compare economic efficiency. Brake Specific Fuel Consumption (BSFC) measures fuel flow rate divided by Brake Power: BSFC = m_dot_f (kg/h) / BP (kW) in kg/kW-h (or g/kW-h). A lower BSFC signifies superior engine efficiency in converting fuel chemical energy into useful mechanical shaft power.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a Morse Test conducted on a 4-cylinder engine, total brake power with all cylinders firing is BP_all. When cylinder 1 is cut out, the remaining cylinders develop BP_1. What is the Indicated Power of cylinder 1 (IP_1)?

options.A: IP_1 = BP_all + BP_1
options.B: IP_1 = BP_all - BP_1
options.C: IP_1 = (BP_all - BP_1) / 4

explanation: The Morse test determines the Indicated Power of high-speed multi-cylinder engines without cylinder pressure indicators. When all cylinders fire: BP_all = (IP1 + IP2 + IP3 + IP4) - (FP1 + FP2 + FP3 + FP4). When cylinder 1 is cut out (shorting spark plug or cutting fuel injection) while speed is restored to test rpm: BP_1 = (0 + IP2 + IP3 + IP4) - (FP1 + FP2 + FP3 + FP4). Assuming engine friction FP remains constant at that speed, subtracting the two gives: IP_1 = BP_all - BP_1. Summing IP for all cylinders gives total IP.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In an internal combustion engine Heat Balance Sheet, what is the approximate percentage distribution of the total heat energy supplied by the fuel (100%)?

options.A: Useful shaft work: 80%; Cooling water: 10%; Exhaust gas: 5%; Radiation: 5%
options.B: Useful shaft work (BP): 30 to 40%; Jacket cooling water: 25 to 30%; Exhaust gas enthalpy: 30 to 35%; Radiation, convection and unaccounted losses: 5 to 10%
options.C: Useful shaft work: 10%; Cooling water: 60%; Exhaust gas: 20%; Radiation: 10%
options.D: Useful shaft work: 50%; Cooling water: 50%; Exhaust gas: 0%

explanation: A Heat Balance Sheet tabulates the accounting of total heat input from fuel combustion (m_dot_f * CV = 100%). In a typical modern internal combustion engine: (1) Heat converted into useful mechanical brake power (BP): approx 30% to 40%; (2) Heat carried away by cylinder jacket cooling water: approx 25% to 30%; (3) Heat carried away by sensible heat in exhaust gases: approx 30% to 35%; (4) Unaccounted losses due to external radiation, convection, and incomplete combustion: approx 5% to 10%.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Positive Displacement Compressor (e.g., reciprocating or screw compressor) from a Dynamic/Rotary Compressor (e.g., centrifugal or axial flow)?

options.A: Positive displacement compressors accelerate air to high kinetic energy and convert it to pressure in a diffuser, while dynamic compressors trap fixed volumes
options.B: Positive displacement compressors trap successive volumes of gas in an enclosed space and mechanically compress it to a smaller volume, delivering high pressure at moderate flow, while dynamic compressors impart kinetic energy via rotating blades for large continuous volume flows
options.C: Dynamic compressors only operate with pure steam and cannot compress atmospheric air
options.D: Reciprocating compressors deliver a completely pulse-free continuous flow at all times

explanation: Positive displacement compressors (reciprocating, vane, screw, roots) physically trap a fixed mass of gas in an expanding/contracting cavity, decreasing its volume mechanically to raise pressure; they are suitable for high pressure ratios and pulsating intermittent/moderate volume flows. Dynamic (rotodynamic) compressors (centrifugal and axial-flow) continuously accelerate gas through high-speed rotating impellers and convert velocity head into static pressure in expanding diffusers; they deliver massive, continuous, pulse-free flow at lower pressure ratios per stage.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: For a single-stage reciprocating air compressor operating without clearance, what is the work done (W) per cycle for polytropic compression (P*V^n = C), and why is Isothermal compression preferred as the thermodynamic ideal?

options.A: W = [n / (n - 1)] * P1 * V1 * [(P2 / P1)^((n - 1) / n) - 1]; Isothermal compression requires the minimum possible work input
options.B: W = [n / (n + 1)] * P1 * V1 * [(P2 / P1)^(n / (n - 1)) - 1]; Isentropic compression requires zero work input
options.C: W = P1 * (V2 - V1); Isochoric compression requires the least power
options.D: W = P1 * V1 * (P2 / P1)^n; Polytropic compression has 100% volumetric efficiency

explanation: Indicated work done per cycle for polytropic compression is the sum of compression work, delivery work, and suction work: W = [n / (n - 1)] * P1 * V1 * [(P2/P1)^((n - 1)/n) - 1]. On a P-V diagram, the area bounded by the compression process and the pressure axis represents work input. Since the isothermal curve (P*V = C) has the lowest slope, it encloses the minimum area, meaning Isothermal compression requires the minimum possible compressor work input. Water jackets and intercoolers are used to approach this isothermal ideal.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: The 'Isothermal Efficiency' (eta_iso) of a reciprocating air compressor is defined as the ratio of:

options.A: Actual shaft work input to adiabatic work output
options.B: Isothermal work input to the Actual indicated work input: eta_iso = W_isothermal / W_indicated
options.C: Delivered volume of air to the swept cylinder volume
options.D: Isentropic work input to polytropic work input

explanation: Because isothermal compression requires the theoretical minimum power to compress gas between given pressure limits, the performance of an air compressor is benchmarked against the isothermal datum. Isothermal efficiency is defined as eta_iso = (Isothermal Work) / (Actual Indicated Work) = [P1 * V1 * ln(P2 / P1)] / W_ind. Higher isothermal efficiency indicates effective heat dissipation through cylinder water jacketing and intercooling.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: The Volumetric Efficiency (eta_v) of a reciprocating air compressor with clearance ratio C = Vc / Vs is given by eta_v = 1 + C - C * (P2 / P1)^(1/n). What happens to volumetric efficiency as the delivery pressure (P2) is increased at constant intake pressure (P1)?

options.A: Volumetric efficiency increases linearly
options.B: Volumetric efficiency decreases, because the high-pressure air trapped in clearance volume expands over a larger portion of the suction stroke before fresh intake can begin
options.C: Volumetric efficiency remains constant regardless of pressure ratio
options.D: Volumetric efficiency reaches 100% at maximum delivery pressure

explanation: Clearance volume Vc traps air at high delivery pressure P2 at the end of delivery. During the return stroke, this trapped clearance air must first re-expand down to suction pressure P1 before the intake valve can open. The higher the delivery pressure P2, the greater the re-expanded clearance volume, leaving a smaller portion of the swept volume (Vs) available for drawing in fresh atmospheric charge. If P2/P1 becomes excessively high, eta_v can drop to zero, setting a practical limit of pressure ratio per stage.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the operational difference between a 'Single-Acting' and a 'Double-Acting' reciprocating compressor running at engine speed N (rpm)?

options.A: Single-acting compresses air in two stages, while double-acting compresses in four stages
options.B: Single-acting admits and compresses air on only one side of the piston (1 delivery stroke per revolution, Q approx L*A*N), while double-acting compresses air alternately on both sides of the piston (2 delivery strokes per revolution, Q approx 2*L*A*N)
options.C: Single-acting requires an intercooler, while double-acting operates without water jackets
options.D: Double-acting compressors have twice the piston speed of single-acting compressors

explanation: In a Single-Acting compressor, the compression process occurs on only one face of the piston (usually the head end), delivering one compressed air charge per crankshaft revolution (n = N). In a Double-Acting compressor, both faces of the piston (head end and crank end) are enclosed in a sealed cylinder with separate suction and delivery valves. Suction occurs on one side while compression and delivery occur simultaneously on the other side, producing two delivery strokes per revolution (n = 2*N) and roughly doubling capacity for the same cylinder bore.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why is 'Multi-Stage Compression with Intercooling' preferred over single-stage compression when delivering air at high pressures (e.g., above 6 to 8 bar)?

options.A: It eliminates the need for air intake filtration
options.B: It saves compression work input, reduces final delivery temperature, improves volumetric efficiency, and allows lighter cylinder construction
options.C: It doubles the polytropic index n to reach adiabatic conditions
options.D: It allows the compressor to run without mechanical lubrication

explanation: Compressing air to high pressures in a single stage causes severe problems: (1) Excessive discharge temperature that vaporizes lubricating oil and risks cylinder explosions; (2) Poor volumetric efficiency due to huge clearance re-expansion; (3) Extremely heavy cylinder walls to withstand peak pressure. Multi-stage compression splits compression across two or more cylinders. Cooling the air between stages in an Intercooler reduces air volume, saving compression work (represented by the intercooler area on the P-V diagram), keeps temperatures safe, and restores high volumetric efficiency.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a Two-Stage reciprocating air compressor with complete (perfect) intercooling, what is the condition for Minimum Total Work input, and what is the relationship between the stage pressures?

options.A: Intermediate pressure Pi = (P1 + P2) / 2; work in low-pressure cylinder is twice that of high-pressure cylinder
options.B: Intermediate pressure Pi = sqrt(P1 * P2); stage pressure ratios are equal (Pi / P1 = P2 / Pi), and work done in both cylinders is equal (W_LP = W_HP)
options.C: Intermediate pressure Pi = P2 / P1; Low pressure work equals zero
options.D: Intermediate pressure Pi = P1 * P2; High pressure cylinder operates at 100% isothermal efficiency

explanation: Total work for a 2-stage compressor with perfect intercooling (air cooled back to initial intake temperature T1) is W_total = [n/(n-1)]*R*T1*[(Pi/P1)^((n-1)/n) + (P2/Pi)^((n-1)/n) - 2]. Differentiating W_total with respect to intermediate pressure Pi and equating to zero yields: Pi / P1 = P2 / Pi => Pi^2 = P1 * P2 => Pi = sqrt(P1 * P2). For minimum total work: (1) Pressure ratio across each stage is identical (rp = sqrt(P2/P1)); (2) Work done is divided equally between low-pressure and high-pressure cylinders (W_LP = W_HP); and (3) Temperature rise in each stage is equal.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Which mode of heat transfer occurs through molecular collision and free electron migration in stationary media without any macroscopic macroscopic bulk movement of matter?

options.A: Convection
options.B: Radiation
options.C: Conduction

explanation: Thermal Conduction is the transfer of internal thermal energy from more energetic particles of a substance to adjacent less energetic ones as a result of interactions between particles (lattice vibrations and free electron transport in solids, and molecular collisions/diffusion in stationary liquids and gases) without gross macroscopic movement of the material. Convection involves bulk fluid motion, while Radiation occurs via electromagnetic waves and requires no material medium.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: According to Fourier's Law of Thermal Conduction, the rate of 1D steady heat conduction (Q) through a plane wall of area A and thickness dx is expressed as Q = -k * A * (dT / dx). What does the negative sign signify?

options.A: Heat is absorbed rather than transmitted across the boundary
options.B: Heat flows in the direction of decreasing temperature (along negative temperature gradient, dT/dx < 0), ensuring Q is positive in the flow direction
options.C: Thermal conductivity k decreases with distance
options.D: The process violates the Second Law of Thermodynamics

explanation: In Fourier's law Q = -k * A * (dT / dx), heat transfer Q must be a positive quantity in the direction of heat flow. According to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, heat naturally flows from a higher temperature to a lower temperature. Therefore, temperature decreases as coordinate distance x increases, making the temperature gradient (dT/dx) negative. The negative sign is introduced to make the resulting heat flow Q mathematically positive in the direction of flow.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the SI unit of Thermal Conductivity (k), and which of the following lists engineering materials in DECREASING order of thermal conductivity at room temperature?

options.A: W / (m^2 * K); Air > Water > Steel > Copper
options.B: W / (m * K); Copper > Aluminium > Steel > Water > Air
options.C: J / (kg * K); Water > Copper > Aluminium > Wood
options.D: N / (m * s); Steel > Aluminium > Copper > Diamond

explanation: From Fourier's law k = Q / [A * (dT/dx)], the SI unit is W / (m^2 * (K/m)) = W / (m * K) (or W / (m * deg C)). Pure metals have very high thermal conductivity due to free electron transport: Copper (approx 385 W/m-K) > Aluminium (approx 205 W/m-K) > Carbon Steel (approx 45 W/m-K). Non-metallic liquids have moderate conductivity: Water (approx 0.6 W/m-K). Gases have very low conductivity due to wide molecular spacing: Air (approx 0.026 W/m-K), making air an excellent thermal insulator when trapped.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How does temperature increase affect the Thermal Conductivity (k) of pure metals and gases, respectively?

options.A: Increases for pure metals, decreases for gases
options.B: Decreases for pure metals, but increases for gases
options.C: Increases for both pure metals and gases
options.D: Decreases for both pure metals and gases

explanation: In pure metals, thermal conduction is dominated by free electron movement. As temperature rises, amplitude of lattice atom vibrations increases, scattering free electrons and impeding their path; hence, thermal conductivity of pure metals decreases with temperature. In gases, thermal conductivity is governed by kinetic molecular collisions: as temperature rises, average molecular velocity increases (proportional to sqrt(T)), increasing collision frequency and energy transport, so gas thermal conductivity increases with temperature.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Newton's Law of Cooling defines convective heat transfer from a solid surface at temperature Ts to a moving ambient fluid at temperature T_inf as Q = h * A * (Ts - T_inf). What is 'h' and its standard SI unit?

options.A: Thermal diffusivity; m^2 / s
options.B: Convective heat transfer coefficient (film coefficient); W / (m^2 * K)
options.C: Stefan-Boltzmann constant; W / (m^2 * K^4)

explanation: In Newton's law of cooling, h is the Convective Heat Transfer Coefficient (also called film coefficient). Its SI unit is W / (m^2 * K). Unlike thermal conductivity k, h is not a thermodynamic material property; it is an empirical parameter that depends strongly on fluid physical properties (viscosity, density, conductivity), surface geometry, and flow hydrodynamics (laminar vs turbulent, natural vs forced convection). Typical values range from 5-25 W/m^2-K for free convection in air, to thousands for boiling or forced water flow.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann Law, the total emissive power (E_b) of an ideal Black Body is directly proportional to which power of its absolute thermodynamic temperature (T)?

options.A: T^1 (proportional to absolute temperature)
options.B: T^2 (proportional to square of temperature)
options.C: T^4 (proportional to fourth power of absolute temperature: E_b = sigma * T^4)

explanation: The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that total hemispherical emissive power of an ideal black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute thermodynamic temperature: E_b = sigma * T^4, where sigma is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W / (m^2 * K^4)) and T is temperature in Kelvin. For a real (grey) surface with emissivity epsilon (0 <= epsilon <= 1), emissive power is E = epsilon * sigma * T^4.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: For heat transfer across a plane composite wall of thickness L and conductivity k bounded by fluid on both sides with convection coefficients h1 and h2, what is the formula for the Overall Heat Transfer Coefficient (U) based on unit area?

options.B: 1 / U = (1 / h1) + (L / k) + (1 / h2) = Sum of Thermal Resistances

explanation: Heat transfer through composite systems is analyzed using thermal resistance analogies (Q = delta_T / R_total). Convective thermal resistance is R_conv = 1 / (h * A) and conductive resistance is R_cond = L / (k * A). Since resistances are in series: R_total = (1 / h1*A) + (L / k*A) + (1 / h2*A). Equating with total heat transfer Q = U * A * delta_T gives 1 / (U * A) = R_total. For unit area A = 1, the overall heat transfer coefficient is given by: 1 / U = (1 / h1) + (L / k) + (1 / h2).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Which of the following thermometric substances is correctly paired with its operating thermometric property used for temperature measurement based on the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics?

options.A: Constant Volume Gas Thermometer - Volume of gas
options.B: Platinum Resistance Thermometer (PRT) - Electrical resistance of wire
options.C: Thermocouple - Length of mercury column
options.D: Constant Pressure Gas Thermometer - Pressure of gas

explanation: According to the Zeroth Law, temperature is measured by observing a physical property that changes reproducibly with temperature. In a Platinum Resistance Thermometer (PRT), the thermometric property is Electrical Resistance (R = R0*(1 + alpha*T)). In a Constant Volume Gas Thermometer, it is Gas Pressure (P). In a Constant Pressure Gas Thermometer, it is Gas Volume (V). In a Thermocouple (Seebeck effect), it is Thermal Electromotive Force (EMF / Voltage).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Which of the following proves that Internal Energy (U) is a thermodynamic property of state (point function) according to the First Law of Thermodynamics?

options.A: The cyclic integral of heat transfer is always zero: integral of delta_Q = 0
options.B: The quantity (delta_Q - delta_W) is identical for all reversible paths connecting two equilibrium states: dU = delta_Q - delta_W, meaning its cyclic integral is zero (integral of dU = 0)
options.C: Internal energy depends directly on the mechanical path taken during expansion
options.D: Work done is independent of the process path

explanation: For any cycle executing paths A and B between states 1 and 2: (Q_A - W_A) = (Q_B - W_B). This proves that the quantity (delta_Q - delta_W) is completely independent of the path followed and depends solely on the initial and final equilibrium states. Therefore, (delta_Q - delta_W) represents the exact differential of a property of state, defined as Internal Energy (dU = delta_Q - delta_W), whose cyclic integral around any closed loop is strictly zero: integral of dU = 0.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Applying the Steady Flow Energy Equation (SFEE) under adiabatic conditions with negligible change in kinetic and potential energy, what are the governing expressions for work done in an expansion Turbine and enthalpy change across a Throttling Valve, respectively?

options.A: Turbine Work W = h1 - h2; Throttling Valve h1 = h2 (isenthalpic)
options.B: Turbine Work W = h2 - h1; Throttling Valve s1 = s2 (isentropic)
options.C: Turbine Work W = u1 - u2; Throttling Valve P1 = P2 (isobaric)
options.D: Turbine Work W = 0; Throttling Valve W = h1 - h2

explanation: The general SFEE per unit mass is h1 + (V1^2 / 2) + g*z1 + q = h2 + (V2^2 / 2) + g*z2 + w. For an adiabatic steam/gas turbine (q = 0, delta_KE approx 0, delta_PE approx 0), work produced is W = h1 - h2. For an adiabatic throttling valve (porous plug or narrow orifice), there is no work transfer (w = 0), no heat transfer (q = 0), and kinetic energy change is negligible, yielding h1 = h2 (a strictly isenthalpic process).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: The Clausius Inequality of the Second Law states that the cyclic integral of (delta_Q / T) around any closed thermodynamic cycle satisfies which criteria for reversible, irreversible, and impossible cycles?

options.B: > 0 for reversible; = 0 for irreversible; < 0 for impossible
options.C: < 0 for reversible; > 0 for irreversible; = 0 for impossible

explanation: The Clausius Inequality states that integral of (delta_Q / T) <= 0 for any thermodynamic cycle. Specifically: (1) If cyclic integral of (delta_Q / T) = 0, the cycle is internally and externally Reversible; (2) If cyclic integral of (delta_Q / T) < 0, the cycle is Irreversible (real cycle); (3) If cyclic integral of (delta_Q / T) > 0, the cycle is Physically Impossible because it violates the Second Law of Thermodynamics.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: According to the Principle of Increase of Entropy, for any spontaneous, naturally occurring process in an isolated system (such as the universe):

options.A: The total entropy of the system remains strictly constant at all times
options.B: The total entropy of the system always increases (delta_S_universe > 0), reaching a maximum at thermodynamic equilibrium
options.C: The total entropy of the system decreases towards absolute zero
options.D: Entropy is converted into available mechanical work without heat rejection

explanation: For an isolated system (which cannot exchange heat or work with surroundings, delta_Q = 0), dS >= delta_Q / T implies dS_isolated >= 0. For an internally reversible process, dS = 0 (isentropic). However, all natural, spontaneous processes are irreversible (due to friction, throttling, unrestrained expansion, or finite temperature gradient heat transfer), which generates entropy: delta_S_gen > 0. Therefore, the entropy of an isolated system (or the universe) always increases: (delta_S)_universe > 0.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the exact mathematical relationship between the Coefficient of Performance of a Heat Pump (COP_HP) and a Refrigerator (COP_Ref) operating between the same high temperature source (T_H) and low temperature sink (T_L)?

options.A: COP_HP = COP_Ref - 1
options.B: COP_HP = COP_Ref + 1
options.C: COP_HP = 1 / COP_Ref

explanation: For a refrigerator, desired output is heat extracted from the cold space Q_L: COP_Ref = Q_L / W_in = Q_L / (Q_H - Q_L). For a heat pump, desired output is heat delivered to the heated space Q_H: COP_HP = Q_H / W_in = Q_H / (Q_H - Q_L). Since Q_H = Q_L + W_in, dividing by W_in yields: COP_HP = (Q_L + W_in) / W_in = (Q_L / W_in) + 1 = COP_Ref + 1. Thus, COP of a heat pump is always strictly greater than that of a refrigerator by exactly 1.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: During the 'Free Expansion' (unresisted expansion into vacuum) of an ideal gas through an insulated valve, which thermodynamic parameters remain constant, and how much work is done?

options.A: Work done W = P1*(V2 - V1); Temperature increases
options.B: Work done W = 0, Heat transfer Q = 0; Internal energy and temperature remain constant (U1 = U2, T1 = T2), but the process is highly irreversible
options.C: Work done W = m*R*T*ln(V2/V1); Entropy generation is zero
options.D: Pressure remains constant; Work done is maximum

explanation: In free expansion, gas expands into an evacuated chamber without overcoming any external resisting boundary force; hence, boundary work done is strictly W = 0. Since the container is insulated, heat transfer Q = 0. From the First Law: Q = delta_U + W => delta_U = 0 => U1 = U2. For an ideal gas (U = m*Cv*T), constant internal energy implies initial temperature equals final temperature (T1 = T2). However, because the expansion is unresisted, it is highly irreversible and generates significant entropy (delta_S = m*R*ln(V2/V1) > 0).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a Throttling process (Joule-Thomson expansion), what is the definition of the Joule-Thomson coefficient (mu_JT), and what condition dictates whether a real gas cools or heats up during throttling?

options.A: mu_JT = (dT / dP)_h; Cooling occurs if mu_JT > 0 (throttling below inversion temperature)
options.B: mu_JT = (dP / dT)_s; Heating occurs if mu_JT > 0
options.C: mu_JT = (dh / dP)_T; Temperature is always constant for all real gases
options.D: mu_JT = (ds / dT)_P; Cooling occurs if mu_JT < 0

explanation: The Joule-Thomson coefficient is the slope of an isenthalpic line on a T-P diagram: mu_JT = (dT / dP)_h. During throttling, pressure always drops (dP < 0). If mu_JT > 0 (region below the inversion curve), a pressure drop produces a temperature drop (dT < 0), causing cooling (used in refrigeration and gas liquefaction). If mu_JT < 0, throttling produces heating. For an ideal gas, mu_JT is strictly zero because enthalpy depends only on temperature.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: When compressing an ideal gas from initial pressure P1 to final pressure P2 in a piston-cylinder device, how do the magnitudes of work input compare among Isothermal, Polytropic (1 < n < gamma), and Isentropic (adiabatic) processes on a P-V diagram?

options.A: W_isentropic < W_polytropic < W_isothermal
options.B: W_isothermal < W_polytropic < W_isentropic
options.C: W_polytropic < W_isothermal < W_isentropic
options.D: Work required is identical for all processes between the same pressure limits

explanation: On a P-V diagram, compression proceeds from higher volume V1 to lower volume V2 across a given pressure rise from P1 to P2. The area under the curve projected onto the pressure axis represents compression work input: W = integral of V dP. Since the isothermal curve has the lowest slope (dP/dV = -P/V), it hugs closest to the volume axis, enclosing the smallest area (minimum work). The isentropic curve is steepest (dP/dV = -gamma*P/V), enclosing the largest area (maximum work). Therefore: W_isothermal < W_polytropic < W_isentropic.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: On thermodynamic coordinate planes, what do the areas under a reversible process curve represent when projected onto the volume axis of a P-V diagram and the entropy axis of a T-s diagram, respectively?

options.A: P-V diagram: Heat transfer; T-s diagram: Boundary work
options.B: P-V diagram: Reversible non-flow boundary work (integral of P dV); T-s diagram: Reversible heat transfer (integral of T ds)
options.C: P-V diagram: Enthalpy change; T-s diagram: Internal energy change
options.D: Both areas represent frictional shaft power

explanation: For a reversible non-flow process: (1) The area under the process curve on a P-V diagram projected onto the horizontal volume axis represents the mechanical boundary displacement work: W = integral of P dV; (2) The area under the process curve on a Temperature-entropy (T-s) diagram projected onto the horizontal entropy axis represents the reversible thermal heat transfer: Q = integral of T ds.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: The general polytropic equation P * V^n = constant represents all standard thermodynamic processes by varying the index 'n'. Which values of 'n' correspond to Isobaric, Isothermal, Isentropic, and Isochoric processes, respectively?

options.A: Isobaric: n = 1; Isothermal: n = 0; Isentropic: n = infinity; Isochoric: n = gamma
options.B: Isobaric: n = 0; Isothermal: n = 1; Isentropic: n = gamma; Isochoric: n = infinity
options.C: Isobaric: n = gamma; Isothermal: n = 1; Isentropic: n = 0; Isochoric: n = infinity
options.D: Isobaric: n = 0; Isothermal: n = gamma; Isentropic: n = 1; Isochoric: n = 2

explanation: For P * V^n = C: (1) When n = 0: P * V^0 = C => P = Constant (Isobaric process); (2) When n = 1: P * V^1 = C => P*V = Constant (Isothermal process for ideal gas); (3) When n = gamma: P * V^gamma = C (Reversible adiabatic / Isentropic process); (4) When n = infinity: P^(1/n) * V = C^(1/n) => P^0 * V = Constant => V = Constant (Isochoric process).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How does the reversible steady-flow work (open system, e.g., in an adiabatic turbine, -integral of V dP) compare to the reversible non-flow work (closed system, integral of P dV) for an isentropic process with index gamma?

options.A: W_open = W_closed
options.B: W_open = gamma * W_closed
options.C: W_open = W_closed / gamma

explanation: For an isentropic process (P*V^gamma = C): Closed system non-flow work is W_closed = integral of P dV = (P1*V1 - P2*V2) / (gamma - 1). Open system steady-flow shaft work is W_open = -integral of V dP = [gamma / (gamma - 1)] * (P1*V1 - P2*V2). Dividing the two expressions reveals that W_open = gamma * W_closed. Because gamma approx 1.4 for air, an isentropic steady-flow turbine extracts 1.4 times the displacement work of a closed cylinder between the same pressure boundaries.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why is the ideal Carnot cycle considered practically impossible to execute in a reciprocating engine, even though it offers the maximum theoretical thermal efficiency?

options.A: Carnot efficiency violates the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
options.B: It requires the isothermal heat transfer processes to be carried out extremely slowly to maintain constant temperature, while the isentropic processes must occur extremely rapidly, resulting in an impractically low Mean Effective Pressure (mep) and massive cylinder size
options.C: Carnot cycle requires liquid mercury as the only working fluid
options.D: The compression ratio must be zero for Carnot cycle to work

explanation: A Carnot engine requires: (1) Isothermal heat addition and rejection, which demand infinite time / ultra-slow piston speed to maintain thermal equilibrium with reservoirs; (2) Isentropic expansion and compression, which require ultra-fast piston speed to prevent heat transfer. Alternating between extremely slow and extremely rapid piston speeds in the same stroke is mechanically impossible. Furthermore, the P-V diagram of a Carnot cycle is very narrow, yielding an extremely small net work area relative to peak pressure, leading to near-zero Mean Effective Pressure (mep) and an impossibly heavy engine.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the concept of 'Mean Effective Pressure' (p_m or mep) in an air standard cycle, and how is it related to net work done (W_net) and swept volume (V_s)?

options.A: p_m = W_net * V_s
options.B: p_m = W_net / V_s (constant fictitious pressure that would produce the same net work output per stroke)
options.C: p_m = V_s / W_net

explanation: Mean Effective Pressure (mep or p_m) is a theoretical, constant fictitious pressure that, if acting uniformly on the piston crown throughout the entire power/expansion stroke (swept volume Vs = V1 - V2), would deliver the identical net work output as the actual varying pressure cycle: W_net = p_m * (V1 - V2) = p_m * V_s => p_m = W_net / V_s. It serves as the primary parameter to evaluate engine specific torque and power independent of cylinder displacement size.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: For an ideal Otto cycle operating on air (gamma = 1.4), if the compression ratio (r) is increased from 6 to 8, what is the approximate increase in air-standard thermal efficiency?

options.A: Increases from approx 51.2% to 56.5%
options.B: Increases from approx 20.0% to 45.0%
options.C: Decreases by 10.5%

explanation: Otto cycle efficiency is eta = 1 - (1 / r^(gamma - 1)). For r1 = 6: eta1 = 1 - (1 / 6^0.4) = 1 - (1 / 2.048) = 1 - 0.488 = 0.512 (51.2%). For r2 = 8: eta2 = 1 - (1 / 8^0.4) = 1 - (1 / 2.297) = 1 - 0.435 = 0.565 (56.5%). Thus, increasing compression ratio from 6 to 8 yields a significant thermal efficiency boost from 51.2% to 56.5%. However, beyond r approx 10 to 12, the rate of efficiency gain diminishes and knocking limits further increase in petrol engines.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In an ideal Dual Combustion cycle with compression ratio r, explosion pressure ratio rp = P3 / P2, and cut-off ratio rho = V4 / V3, what is the effect on thermal efficiency if the explosion pressure ratio (rp) is increased at constant compression ratio and constant cut-off ratio?

options.A: Efficiency decreases to zero
options.B: Efficiency increases, because a greater fraction of heat is added at constant volume at the highest density
options.C: Efficiency remains unchanged

explanation: In the Dual combustion cycle efficiency formula: eta_Dual = 1 - (1 / r^(gamma - 1)) * [ (rp * rho^gamma - 1) / ((rp - 1) + gamma * rp * (rho - 1)) ]. Increasing the explosion pressure ratio rp means that more heat is released during the constant-volume phase rather than during constant-pressure expansion. Constant-volume heat addition at TDC achieves higher peak temperature and expansion ratio, which increases thermodynamic thermal efficiency.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In an ideal Joule (Brayton) gas turbine cycle operating between minimum atmospheric temperature T1 and maximum metallurgical turbine inlet temperature T3, what is the optimum pressure ratio (rp,opt) that maximizes the Net Specific Work output?

options.A: rp,opt = (T3 / T1)
options.B: rp,opt = (T3 / T1)^(gamma / (2 * (gamma - 1)))
options.C: rp,opt = sqrt(T3 / T1)

explanation: Net work in a Brayton cycle is W_net = Cp * [(T3 - T4) - (T2 - T1)]. Expressing intermediate temperatures in terms of pressure ratio rp: W_net = Cp * [T3*(1 - 1/rp^x) - T1*(rp^x - 1)], where x = (gamma - 1) / gamma. Differentiating W_net with respect to rp and setting dW/drp = 0 yields: rp^x = sqrt(T3 / T1) => rp,opt = (T3 / T1)^(1 / (2*x)) = (T3 / T1)^(gamma / (2 * (gamma - 1))). At this optimum pressure ratio, compressor discharge temperature equals turbine exhaust temperature (T2 = T4 = sqrt(T1 * T3)).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How does the value of the adiabatic index / specific heat ratio (gamma = Cp / Cv) affect the air-standard efficiency of an Otto cycle at a given compression ratio r (e.g., comparing Monatomic gas gamma = 1.67, Diatomic gas gamma = 1.4, and Triatomic gas gamma = 1.33)?

options.A: Higher gamma produces higher thermal efficiency: eta_monatomic > eta_diatomic > eta_triatomic
options.B: Lower gamma produces higher thermal efficiency: eta_triatomic > eta_diatomic > eta_monatomic
options.C: Gamma has zero influence on Otto cycle efficiency
options.D: Monatomic and triatomic gases have identical efficiencies

explanation: From the Otto cycle efficiency formula eta = 1 - (1 / r^(gamma - 1)), the term (gamma - 1) appears directly in the exponent of compression ratio r in the denominator. As gamma increases, (gamma - 1) increases, which makes r^(gamma - 1) larger and reduces the rejected heat fraction 1 / r^(gamma - 1). Consequently, for a given compression ratio r: a monatomic gas (e.g., Argon, Helium with gamma = 1.67) yields the highest thermal efficiency, followed by a diatomic gas (e.g., Air, N2 with gamma = 1.4), while triatomic gases (e.g., CO2 with gamma = 1.33) have the lowest efficiency.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Theoretically, for the same cylinder dimensions and engine speed, a two-stroke engine produces twice the power of a four-stroke engine. In practice, however, its actual power output is only about 1.5 to 1.7 times that of a four-stroke engine. What is the primary reason?

options.A: Higher mechanical bearing friction in two-stroke engines
options.B: Loss of fresh charge during scavenging, reduced effective compression/expansion stroke due to open ports, and poor combustion efficiency
options.C: Lower operating temperature of two-stroke engines
options.D: Inability to operate with standard lubricating oils

explanation: In a 2-stroke engine: (1) Cylinder ports occupy a significant portion of the lower cylinder barrel, so effective compression and expansion strokes are shorter than total piston stroke; (2) During scavenging, a fraction of fresh charge escapes directly through the open exhaust port (short-circuiting); (3) High residual exhaust gas dilution impairs combustion efficiency; and (4) Greater thermal loading causes thermal throttling, resulting in actual power output of 1.5 to 1.7 times rather than the theoretical 2 times.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: On the actual P-V indicator diagram of a naturally aspirated four-stroke internal combustion engine, what is the 'Pumping Loop' and why does it represent negative work?

options.A: The area enclosed by the compression and power curves; represents net shaft work
options.B: The lower loop enclosed between the exhaust line and suction line; pressure during exhaust is above atmospheric and suction is below atmospheric, requiring work input from the engine
options.C: The area under the isentropic expansion curve
options.D: The loop formed during fuel injection

explanation: In a naturally aspirated 4-stroke engine, suction occurs below ambient atmospheric pressure (partial vacuum to draw in charge) while exhaust occurs slightly above atmospheric pressure (to push out burned gases). The lower loop on the indicator diagram traced by exhaust and suction lines runs in a counter-clockwise direction, representing 'Pumping Loss' (negative work done by the piston on the gases). In a supercharged engine with boost pressure exceeding exhaust backpressure, this loop reverses to clockwise and delivers positive pumping work.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How is fresh air-fuel mixture pre-compressed in a conventional small two-stroke petrol engine before entering the cylinder through the transfer port?

options.A: By an external exhaust-driven turbocharger
options.B: In the sealed crankcase beneath the piston during the downward power stroke (Crankcase Scavenging)
options.C: By an electric air pump mounted on the cylinder head
options.D: By thermal expansion in the exhaust muffler

explanation: Small two-stroke engines utilize Crankcase Compression (crankcase scavenging). The crankcase is hermetically sealed. As the piston travels upward during compression, pressure in the crankcase drops, pulling in fresh charge through the inlet port/reed valve. As the piston travels downward on the power stroke, its underside compresses the trapped charge in the crankcase. When the descending piston uncovers the transfer port, this pre-compressed charge rushes into the cylinder above.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the functional purpose of a 'Deflector' (hump) on the crown of a piston in a cross-scavenged two-stroke engine?

options.A: To increase the structural weight of the reciprocating assembly
options.B: To deflect the incoming fresh charge upward toward the cylinder head, preventing it from rushing directly across into the opposite open exhaust port
options.C: To provide a mounting location for the spark plug
options.D: To increase the clearance volume to reduce compression ratio

explanation: In cross-scavenging, the transfer port and exhaust port are positioned directly opposite each other on the cylinder walls. If a flat-top piston were used, the incoming fresh charge would shoot directly across the cylinder bore into the open exhaust port (short-circuiting). A deflector hump on the piston crown redirects the incoming fresh charge vertically toward the cylinder head, creating a sweeping loop that flushes out exhaust gases while minimizing fresh fuel loss.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Comparing flywheels for a two-stroke engine and a four-stroke engine of identical rated power and speed, why can the two-stroke engine use a significantly smaller and lighter flywheel?

options.A: The two-stroke engine runs at higher linear piston speed
options.B: The two-stroke engine produces a power stroke every single crankshaft revolution (360 deg) compared to every two revolutions (720 deg) in a four-stroke engine, resulting in a much smaller coefficient of fluctuation of energy
options.C: Two-stroke engines do not require balancing weights on the crankshaft
options.D: The four-stroke engine operates with zero torque fluctuation

explanation: Flywheel size depends on the Maximum Fluctuation of Energy (delta_E) on the turning moment diagram: Mass m proportional to delta_E / (R^2 * omega^2 * C_s). In a 4-stroke engine, one power stroke is separated by three idle strokes across 720 degrees, producing severe torque peaks and valleys that require a massive flywheel. In a 2-stroke engine, a power stroke occurs every 360 degrees (twice as frequently), making torque delivery far more uniform and drastically reducing delta_E, allowing a much lighter flywheel.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: The 'Volumetric Efficiency' of a four-stroke internal combustion engine is defined as the ratio of:

options.A: Swept volume to total cylinder volume
options.B: Actual mass of fresh air inducted into the cylinder during suction to the theoretical mass of air that would occupy the swept volume at ambient atmospheric density
options.C: Brake power to indicated power

explanation: Volumetric efficiency eta_v = (m_act / m_th) = (Actual mass of air aspirated per cycle) / (rho_atm * V_s). It measures the breathing ability of an engine. In naturally aspirated engines, flow friction through air filters, throttle valves, intake ports, and intake manifold heating limits eta_v to typical values of 75% to 85%. Forced induction (supercharging/turbocharging) compresses the intake charge, allowing volumetric efficiencies to exceed 100% to 150%.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In the actual Valve Timing Diagram of a 4-stroke high-speed internal combustion engine, why is the Inlet Valve opened (IVO) 10 to 30 degrees BEFORE Top Dead Center (TDC)?

options.A: To allow combustion flame to travel back into the intake manifold
options.B: To ensure the inlet valve achieves an adequate opening cross-sectional area by the time the piston begins descending and reaches maximum suction velocity
options.C: To reduce the engine mechanical compression ratio
options.D: To cool down the spark plug electrodes before firing

explanation: Mechanical valves cannot open instantaneously; cam profiles require finite angular rotation to lift the valve off its seat. Opening the inlet valve 10 to 30 degrees before TDC ensures that by the time the piston reaches TDC and accelerates downward on the suction stroke, the valve has already reached a substantial flow area, minimizing throttling resistance at the valve curtain and maximizing air induction.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why is the Exhaust Valve opened (EVO) 40 to 60 degrees BEFORE Bottom Dead Center (BDC) on the power stroke in a 4-stroke engine?

options.A: To completely stop the piston before BDC
options.B: To allow the high-pressure combustion gases to rapidly discharge under their own pressure (exhaust blowdown), dropping cylinder pressure to near atmospheric by BDC and reducing piston pumping resistance during the exhaust stroke
options.C: To prevent the engine from developing excessive brake torque
options.D: To inject lubricating oil into the exhaust manifold

explanation: Toward the end of the expansion stroke, the rate of work done by expanding gases decreases significantly. Opening the exhaust valve 40 to 60 degrees before BDC allows high-pressure exhaust gases to vent spontaneously to the atmosphere under sonic/subsonic pressure drop (Exhaust Blowdown). By the time the piston reaches BDC, cylinder pressure has dropped near atmospheric, greatly reducing the mechanical pumping work required by the piston to expel the remaining gases during the upward exhaust stroke.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a four-stroke internal combustion engine, what is the primary thermodynamic reason for keeping the Exhaust Valve open (EVC) 10 to 20 degrees AFTER Top Dead Center (TDC)?

options.A: To allow lubricating oil to drain into the crankcase
options.B: To utilize the exit momentum and kinetic energy of the high-velocity exhaust gas column to scavenge remaining residual gases from the clearance volume
options.C: To warm up the incoming air-fuel mixture during cold starts
options.D: To prevent the exhaust valve spring from fatiguing

explanation: The high-velocity column of exhaust gases rushing through the exhaust port possesses substantial momentum and kinetic inertia. Keeping the exhaust valve open slightly past TDC allows this moving column of gas to exert a dynamic scavenging suction on the cylinder clearance volume, pulling out residual burnt gases without mechanical work and improving cylinder scavenging efficiency.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In the Port Timing Diagram of a two-stroke engine, what is the 'Exhaust Lead'?

options.A: The distance the exhaust pipe extends beyond the motorcycle frame
options.B: The angular period of crankshaft rotation between the opening of the Exhaust Port and the subsequent opening of the Transfer Port
options.C: The angle between spark ignition and fuel injection
options.D: The duration during which the inlet port is closed

explanation: On the downward stroke in a two-stroke engine, the piston uncovers the exhaust port before the transfer port. The angular difference between the opening of the exhaust port (e.g., 60 deg before BDC) and the opening of the transfer port (e.g., 45 deg before BDC) is called the Exhaust Lead (typically 15 to 25 degrees of crank angle). This timing window ensures that cylinder pressure drops below crankcase pressure before the transfer port opens, preventing high-pressure exhaust gas from blowing back into the crankcase.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the engineering benefit of Variable Valve Timing (VVT) systems in modern automotive internal combustion engines?

options.A: It eliminates the requirement for a cooling radiator
options.B: It continuously optimizes valve opening/closing angles and valve overlap across engine speeds, providing smooth idle with low emissions at low rpm, and high volumetric efficiency with maximum torque at high rpm
options.C: It converts a petrol engine into a diesel engine at high speeds
options.D: It maintains constant valve lift regardless of engine load

explanation: Fixed valve timing represents a compromise between low-speed stability and high-speed breathing. At low rpm, late IVC and high valve overlap cause charge backflow into the intake manifold, leading to rough idling and high unburned hydrocarbon emissions. At high rpm, high overlap and late IVC are essential to harness gas inertia. VVT electronically rotates the camshaft relative to the crankshaft, optimizing valve timing across the entire speed band.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why must the electric spark in a petrol engine (or fuel injection in a diesel engine) occur with an 'Advance' (15 to 35 degrees before TDC) rather than precisely at TDC?

options.A: Because fuel combustion requires zero time to complete
options.B: Because combustion is a progressive chemical reaction requiring finite time (approx 1.5 to 2 milliseconds); advancing ignition ensures that peak cylinder pressure occurs around 10 to 15 degrees after TDC for maximum mechanical torque
options.C: To ensure fuel droplets freeze before ignition starts
options.D: To prevent the piston from crossing TDC

explanation: Combustion does not occur instantaneously; it involves an ignition delay phase followed by turbulent flame propagation taking about 1.5 to 2 ms (or 30 to 40 degrees of crank rotation at 3000 rpm). If ignition were initiated at TDC, peak pressure would occur far down the expansion stroke where cylinder volume has already expanded, severely reducing work output. Spark advance ensures the pressure rise peaks at roughly 10 to 15 degrees after TDC, producing maximum useful torque on the crank slider mechanism.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What are the three recognized stages of normal combustion in a Spark Ignition (SI) petrol engine?

options.A: Physical delay, Chemical delay, and Exhaust blowdown
options.B: (1) Ignition lag (pre-flame chemical reaction period); (2) Turbulent flame propagation across the combustion chamber; (3) Afterburning of residual fuel
options.C: Vaporization, Atomization, and Condensation

explanation: Normal combustion in an SI engine proceeds in three distinct stages: (1) Ignition Lag / Delay Period: The time between spark firing and the establishment of a self-sustaining flame kernel with measurable pressure rise; (2) Flame Propagation: The turbulent flame front sweeps across the combustion chamber, consuming most of the air-fuel mixture and generating the main pressure rise; (3) Afterburning: Continued slow combustion of fuel trapped in boundary quench zones and crevice volumes during early expansion.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the fundamental physical mechanism of 'Knocking' (Detonation) in a Spark Ignition (petrol) engine?

options.A: Pre-ignition occurring before the spark plug fires
options.B: Spontaneous auto-ignition of the unburned 'end-gas' mixture ahead of the advancing flame front due to prolonged exposure to high temperature and compressive radiant heating
options.C: Failure of the intake valve to close before expansion
options.D: Water condensation inside the carburetor bowl

explanation: In an SI engine, as the normal flame front sweeps across the chamber, it compresses and radiantly heats the remaining unburned charge (the end-gas). If the end-gas reaches its auto-ignition temperature and completes its chemical delay period before the flame front arrives, the entire end-gas detonates instantaneously. This produces localized supersonic shock waves (violent knocking sounds), extreme localized temperatures, piston crown erosion, and spark plug melting.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the 'Octane Number' of a spark-ignition fuel, and what reference hydrocarbons define the rating scale of 0 and 100?

options.A: Measures volatility; n-hexane = 0 and benzene = 100
options.B: Measures anti-knock resistance; n-heptane is assigned 0 (highly prone to knock) and Iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) is assigned 100 (highly knock-resistant)
options.C: Measures density; kerosene = 0 and diesel = 100
options.D: Measures calorific value; ethanol = 0 and methane = 100

explanation: Octane rating measures a fuel's resistance to detonation/knocking in SI engines. The primary reference fuels are: (1) Normal-heptane (n-C7H16), which knocks severely and is assigned an Octane Number of 0; (2) Iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane), which exhibits high anti-knock resistance and is assigned an Octane Number of 100. A fuel rated Octane 90 behaves identically in anti-knock quality to a blend of 90% iso-octane and 10% n-heptane by volume.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What are the four successive stages of combustion in a Compression Ignition (Diesel) engine?

options.A: (1) Ignition delay period; (2) Rapid / uncontrolled combustion; (3) Controlled combustion; (4) Afterburning
options.B: (1) Suction; (2) Compression; (3) Expansion; (4) Exhaust
options.C: (1) Vapor lock; (2) Throttling; (3) Scavenging; (4) Detonation

explanation: In a CI engine, liquid fuel is injected into hot compressed air, resulting in four stages: (1) Ignition Delay: Time between start of injection and onset of combustion, consisting of physical delay (atomization/vaporization/mixing) and chemical delay (pre-flame oxidation); (2) Period of Rapid (Uncontrolled) Combustion: The fuel accumulated during the delay period auto-ignites nearly simultaneously, causing an abrupt pressure surge; (3) Period of Controlled Combustion: Injected fuel burns at a rate controlled by injection and air mixing; (4) Afterburning: Continued burning of unmixed fuel and carbon particles during expansion.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is 'Diesel Knock', how does it differ from Petrol (SI) Knock, and what causes it?

options.A: Diesel knock occurs at the end of combustion due to spark failure
options.B: Diesel knock occurs at the start of combustion caused by an excessively long ignition delay period during which excessive fuel accumulates and burns violently all at once, whereas SI knock occurs at the end of combustion
options.C: Diesel knock occurs only when using high cetane fuels
options.D: Diesel knock occurs when compression ratio is too high

explanation: The mechanics of knocking in SI and CI engines are fundamentally opposite: In an SI engine, knock occurs at the END of combustion due to auto-ignition of the unburned end gas. In a CI engine, knock occurs at the START of combustion (during stage 2). If the ignition delay period is too long, a large mass of fuel is injected and vaporized in the chamber before ignition starts; when it finally ignites, this huge fuel mass burns violently in a massive explosion, producing extreme dP/dt and heavy mechanical vibration (Diesel Knock). A short delay period prevents diesel knock.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the 'Cetane Number' of a diesel fuel, and how does it relate to ignition delay and engine knocking?

options.A: A measure of carbon residue; higher cetane increases ignition delay and promotes knock
options.B: A measure of ignition quality and delay period; a higher Cetane number indicates a shorter ignition delay period and smoother knock-free combustion
options.C: A measure of sulfur content in heavy fuel oils
options.D: A dimensionless ratio identical to octane number

explanation: Cetane number measures the ignition readiness of a diesel fuel under compression. Reference fuels are Cetane (n-hexadecane, C16H34, assigned 100 due to very short ignition delay) and alpha-methylnaphthalene (assigned 15, or heptamethylnonane). A higher cetane number means shorter ignition delay, preventing dangerous fuel accumulation in the cylinder and ensuring smooth, quiet, knock-free operation with easy cold-starting.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Which of the following is an example of an 'Absorption Dynamometer' used to measure the Brake Power of an engine by dissipating power into heat?

options.A: Epicyclic train dynamometer
options.B: Prony Brake and Rope Brake dynamometers
options.C: Torsion dynamometer

explanation: Dynamometers are classified into two broad categories: (1) Absorption Dynamometers: Absorb the entire shaft power output of the engine and convert it into heat via mechanical friction (Prony brake, Rope brake), fluid friction (Froude hydraulic dynamometer), or eddy currents (Eddy current dynamometer); (2) Transmission Dynamometers: Measure torque while transmitting mechanical power to an operating driven machine (e.g., Torsion dynamometer, Epicyclic train dynamometer).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a Rope Brake Dynamometer, dead load is W (N), spring balance reading is S (N), brake drum diameter is D (m), rope diameter is d (m), and engine speed is N (rpm). What is the formula for Brake Power (BP) in kW?
explanation: Effective tangential braking force on the drum rim is F_net = (W - S) Newtons. Effective radius of the brake is R_eff = (D + d) / 2 meters. The braking torque is T = F_net * R_eff = (W - S) * (D + d) / 2 N-m. Brake power is BP = (2 * pi * N * T) / 60,000 kW = [2 * pi * N * (W - S) * (D + d) / 2] / 60,000 = [pi * (D + d) * N * (W - S)] / 60,000 kW.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How does a Froude Hydraulic Dynamometer absorb engine brake power, and how does the power absorbed scale with rotational speed (N) and rotor diameter (D)?

options.A: By dry friction between bronze pads; power scales as N^1 and D^2
options.B: By fluid friction and turbulent shear vortices created in water circulating between rotor pockets and stator casings; power absorbed is proportional to N^3 and D^5
options.C: By magnetic hysteresis; power is independent of speed
options.D: By piezoelectric crystal deformation; power scales as N^2 and D^3

explanation: In a hydraulic dynamometer, a rotor with elliptical pockets spins inside a water-filled stator with matching opposing pockets. The high-speed water vortices sheared between rotor and stator absorb the engine's mechanical work through intense fluid friction and turbulence, converting shaft power into thermal energy carried away by continuous cooling water. Dimensional analysis shows power absorbed varies as Power proportional to rho * N^3 * D^5.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How is Indicated Mean Effective Pressure (P_mi) evaluated from an engine indicator diagram having closed loop area 'a' (cm^2), diagram base length 'L' (cm), and indicator spring scale 's' (bar per cm)?

options.A: P_mi = (a * L) / s
options.B: P_mi = (a / L) * s
options.C: P_mi = (L / a) * s

explanation: The area 'a' of the indicator diagram represents work done per cycle to scale, and length 'L' represents stroke volume to scale. The average ordinate height of the indicator diagram is h_avg = Area / Base length = a / L (in cm). Multiplying the average height by the indicator spring scale 's' (which calibrates vertical deflection into pressure, bar/cm) yields the Indicated Mean Effective Pressure: P_mi = (a / L) * s (in bar).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In the 'Motoring Test' for evaluating the Frictional Power (FP) of a single-cylinder engine, how is the test executed?

options.A: The engine is run on pure hydrogen at maximum speed
options.B: The engine is driven (motored) at test operating speed by a coupled electric dynamometer immediately after cutting off fuel/ignition, and the electrical power drawn by the motor is measured as FP
options.C: The engine is run without lubricating oil until it stalls
options.D: The cylinder head is removed and the crank is spun by hand

explanation: The engine is first run under firing conditions until operating temperatures and pressures stabilize. Fuel/ignition is then immediately cut off, and a coupled calibrated DC electric motor drives (motors) the unfired engine at the exact same rotational speed (rpm). The electrical power input required to motor the engine against piston ring friction, bearing friction, and pumping work represents Frictional Power: FP = Power_motoring.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the 'Willans Line Method' for determining engine frictional power, and to which type of engine is it primarily applicable?

options.A: A plot of fuel consumption vs Brake Power for a Compression Ignition (Diesel) engine; extrapolating the line back to zero fuel consumption gives FP on the negative BP axis
options.B: A plot of exhaust temperature vs speed for a petrol engine
options.C: A line connecting spark advance to octane rating
options.D: A plot of cooling water flow rate vs indicated power

explanation: In a CI (diesel) engine running at constant speed, qualitative governing injects fuel in direct proportion to load. A graph of Total Fuel Consumption (kg/h) plotted against Brake Power (kW) forms a nearly straight line known as the Willans Line. Extrapolating this straight line backward to intersect the horizontal Brake Power axis at zero fuel consumption yields the Frictional Power (FP) on the negative BP axis. It is not applicable to throttled petrol engines because manifold vacuum changes pumping losses with load.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: A 4-cylinder, 4-stroke petrol engine running at 3000 rpm develops a torque of 160 N-m. If the indicated mean effective pressure is 8 bar, bore is 80 mm, stroke is 100 mm, what is the Mechanical Efficiency of the engine?
explanation: Step 1: Brake Power BP = 2 * pi * N * T / 60,000 = (2 * pi * 3000 * 160) / 60,000 = 50.27 kW. Step 2: For 4-stroke engine, power strokes n = N/2 = 1500. Piston area A = (pi/4)*(0.08)^2 = 0.005026 m^2. Stroke L = 0.1 m. Indicated Power IP = (P_mi * 100 * L * A * n * k) / 60 = (8 * 100 * 0.1 * 0.005026 * 1500 * 4) / 60 = 60.31 kW. Step 3: Mechanical efficiency eta_m = BP / IP = 50.27 / 60.31 = 0.8335 (83.35%).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: The 'Relative Efficiency' (Efficiency Ratio) of an internal combustion engine is defined as the ratio of:

options.A: Indicated thermal efficiency to mechanical efficiency
options.B: Actual thermal efficiency to the ideal air-standard cycle efficiency: eta_rel = eta_thermal / eta_air_standard
options.C: Volumetric efficiency to swept volume
options.D: Brake specific fuel consumption to indicated power

explanation: Relative Efficiency measures how closely an actual engine approaches the theoretical thermodynamic ideal of its air-standard cycle: eta_rel = (Actual Indicated or Brake Thermal Efficiency) / (Air-Standard Cycle Efficiency). It is always less than 1 (typically 0.6 to 0.8) due to real-gas effects: dissociation of CO2 and H2O at high temperatures, variation of specific heats with temperature, progressive combustion, heat loss to cooling jackets, and blowdown losses.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the exact mathematical relationship between Indicated Specific Fuel Consumption (ISFC), Brake Specific Fuel Consumption (BSFC), and Mechanical Efficiency (eta_m)?

options.A: ISFC = BSFC * eta_m
options.B: ISFC = BSFC / eta_m
options.C: BSFC = ISFC * eta_m

explanation: By definition, BSFC = m_dot_f / BP and ISFC = m_dot_f / IP. Since mechanical efficiency is eta_m = BP / IP, we have BP = eta_m * IP. Substituting BP into BSFC: BSFC = m_dot_f / (eta_m * IP) = (1 / eta_m) * (m_dot_f / IP) = ISFC / eta_m. Rearranging gives: ISFC = BSFC * eta_m. Because eta_m < 1, ISFC is always numerically lower than BSFC.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the chemically correct (stoichiometric) Air-Fuel ratio for complete combustion of commercial petrol (gasoline), and what mixture ratios are required for cold starting vs maximum cruise economy?

options.A: Stoichiometric approx 14.7:1; Cold starting approx 3:1 to 5:1 (very rich); Cruise economy approx 16:1 to 18:1 (lean)
options.B: Stoichiometric approx 5:1; Cold starting approx 14.7:1; Cruise economy approx 25:1
options.C: Stoichiometric approx 20:1; Cold starting approx 20:1; Cruise economy approx 10:1
options.D: Air-fuel ratio is always 1:1 by volume across all engine regimes

explanation: For commercial gasoline (approx C8H18), theoretical complete combustion requires a stoichiometric A/F ratio of approx 14.7:1 by mass. However: (1) Cold starting requires a very rich mixture (3:1 to 5:1) because only light volatile fractions vaporize at low engine temperatures; (2) Idling requires a rich mixture (10:1 to 12:1) due to exhaust dilution; (3) Maximum power demands slightly rich (12:1 to 13:1); (4) Maximum fuel economy requires a lean mixture (16:1 to 18:1).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why do Compression Ignition (Diesel) engines operate with very lean overall air-fuel ratios (ranging from 18:1 at full load to over 80:1 at idle)?

options.A: Because diesel fuel has a higher density than gasoline
options.B: Because diesel fuel is injected directly into the cylinder near TDC and combustion is heterogeneous (diffusion flame); excess air is mandatory to ensure injected fuel droplets find oxygen before entering the exhaust
options.C: Because diesel engines cannot breathe ambient air without an intake throttle

explanation: In a CI engine, there is no premixed air-fuel charge; fuel is sprayed as liquid droplets directly into the combustion chamber just before TDC. Combustion is heterogeneous: fuel droplets vaporize and burn in local diffusion flames. Because fuel-air mixing time is extremely short (milliseconds), large excess air is essential (overall lean mixture 20:1 to 80:1). If a diesel engine were run near stoichiometric (14.5:1), lack of local oxygen would generate intense black smoke (soot/particulate matter).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How does load regulation (governing) differ between a Spark Ignition (Petrol) engine and a Compression Ignition (Diesel) engine?

options.A: SI engines use Qualitative governing; CI engines use Quantitative governing
options.B: SI engines use Quantitative governing (throttle valve regulates total mixture quantity while A/F ratio remains relatively constant); CI engines use Qualitative governing (fuel injection quantity is varied while air intake is completely unthrottled)
options.C: Both engines throttle the intake air identically
options.D: Both engines govern speed by varying ignition timing only

explanation: In an SI (petrol) engine, a throttle valve controls the total mass of homogeneous air-fuel mixture admitted into the cylinders (Quantitative governing), keeping the mixture ratio close to combustible limits (11:1 to 16:1). In a CI (diesel) engine, air intake is wide open and unthrottled at all times (full volumetric air induction); the governor varies only the volume of diesel fuel injected per stroke (Qualitative governing), varying the mixture strength from very lean at idle to richer at full load.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the critical operating assumption made in the Morse Test when calculating the Indicated Power of each individual cylinder?

options.A: Engine speed drops to zero during the test
options.B: The engine frictional power (FP) of the cut-off cylinder and running cylinders remains unchanged when one cylinder is cut out, provided engine speed is restored to test rpm
options.C: Specific fuel consumption decreases linearly with cut-out cylinders
options.D: The compression ratio of the cut-out cylinder increases to infinity

explanation: The Morse test assumes that total engine friction power (FP) is primarily a function of rotational speed (rpm). When one cylinder is disabled (spark shorted or fuel cut) and the dynamometer load is rapidly reduced to bring engine speed back to exactly the original test rpm, the mechanical friction of the pistons, rings, bearings, and valve gear is assumed to remain constant. Thus, the observed drop in Brake Power equals the Indicated Power of that cut-off cylinder.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a Morse test on a 4-cylinder engine running at constant speed, total Brake Power with all cylinders working is 40 kW. When cylinders 1, 2, 3, and 4 are cut out one by one, the recorded brake powers are 28 kW, 28.5 kW, 27.5 kW, and 28 kW, respectively. What is the total Indicated Power (IP) and Mechanical Efficiency?

options.A: IP = 48 kW; Mechanical efficiency = 83.3%
options.B: IP = 38 kW; Mechanical efficiency = 95.0%
options.C: IP = 55 kW; Mechanical efficiency = 72.7%

explanation: Step 1: Calculate IP for each cylinder using IP_i = BP_all - BP_without_i: IP1 = 40 - 28 = 12 kW; IP2 = 40 - 28.5 = 11.5 kW; IP3 = 40 - 27.5 = 12.5 kW; IP4 = 40 - 28 = 12 kW. Step 2: Total IP = IP1 + IP2 + IP3 + IP4 = 12 + 11.5 + 12.5 + 12 = 48 kW. Step 3: Total Frictional Power FP = Total IP - BP_all = 48 - 40 = 8 kW. Step 4: Mechanical efficiency eta_m = BP_all / Total IP = 40 / 48 = 0.8333 (83.33%).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why is it physically impossible to conduct a Morse Test on a Single-Cylinder internal combustion engine?

options.A: Because a single-cylinder engine does not have an intake valve
options.B: Because cutting off the fuel or spark to the only cylinder immediately stalls and stops the engine completely, leaving no other cylinders to motor the engine against friction at operating speed
options.C: Because a single-cylinder engine has zero frictional power
options.D: Because the Morse test is only valid for rotary Wankel engines

explanation: The Morse test relies on cutting off power generation in one cylinder while the remaining active cylinders continue to fire and drive the engine at the designated test speed against the cut cylinder's friction. In a single-cylinder engine, there are no other cylinders to maintain rotation; killing the spark or fuel immediately stalls the engine. Hence, frictional power in single-cylinder engines must be measured via Motoring Test or Willans line.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: How is a cylinder disabled during a Morse test on a Compression Ignition (Diesel) engine as compared to a Spark Ignition (Petrol) engine?

options.A: SI engine: Throttle closed; CI engine: Air intake plugged
options.B: SI engine: Spark plug electrical lead is shorted/grounded; CI engine: High-pressure fuel injection pipe union is loosened (or fuel rack held) to cut off fuel supply to that injector
options.C: SI engine: Valve spring removed; CI engine: Piston removed
options.D: Both engines cut ignition by turning off the battery switch

explanation: In an SI (petrol) engine, a cylinder is cut out by short-circuiting its spark plug to the engine block using an insulated screwdriver or grounded switch. In a CI (diesel) engine, which has no spark plugs, the cylinder is cut out by unscrewing the delivery union nut on the high-pressure fuel line between the injection pump and the injector (allowing fuel to spill into a container) or by manually latching the fuel pump rack for that plunger.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In an engine performance trial, fuel consumption is 6 kg/h with calorific value 42,000 kJ/kg. If the engine develops a Brake Power of 24 kW, what percentage of the total heat supplied is converted into useful brake work?
explanation: Step 1: Total heat supplied by fuel per hour Q_in = m_f * CV = 6 kg/h * 42,000 kJ/kg = 252,000 kJ/h. In kW: Q_in = 252,000 / 3600 = 70 kW. Step 2: Useful shaft heat equivalent to Brake Power is Q_BP = 24 kW (or 24 * 3600 = 86,400 kJ/h). Step 3: Percentage of heat converted to brake power = (Q_BP / Q_in) * 100 = (24 / 70) * 100 = 34.28% (approx 34.3%).

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: In a Heat Balance Sheet calculation, how is the 'Heat carried away by Exhaust Gases' (Q_exhaust) evaluated using mass of exhaust gas m_g (kg/min), specific heat C_pg (kJ/kg-K), exhaust temperature T_g, and ambient temperature T_a?

options.A: Q_exhaust = m_g * C_pg * (T_g - T_a)
options.B: Q_exhaust = m_g * C_pg * (T_g + T_a)
options.C: Q_exhaust = m_g * (T_g - T_a) / C_pg

explanation: The sensible heat carried away in dry exhaust gas products is determined by measuring exhaust gas temperature (T_g) via a pyrometer and knowing ambient intake air temperature (T_a). Using mass flow rate of exhaust gas (m_g = m_air + m_fuel): Q_exhaust = m_g * C_pg * (T_g - T_a) kJ/min (or kJ/s). Moisture formed by combustion of fuel hydrogen also carries latent heat of vaporization.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the primary thermodynamic objective of 'Supercharging' an internal combustion engine?

options.A: To reduce cylinder peak pressure to atmospheric levels
options.B: To supply the intake air at a pressure and density higher than surrounding ambient atmosphere, allowing a greater mass of oxygen to burn more fuel and produce significantly higher power output without increasing engine displacement volume
options.C: To completely eliminate the need for an exhaust manifold
options.D: To decrease the mean effective pressure of the cycle

explanation: Engine power is fundamentally limited by the mass of air inducted per cycle. Supercharging uses an air blower or compressor to force dense air into the cylinders at pressures typically 0.5 to 2 bar above atmospheric. This allows proportionally more fuel to be burned completely per power stroke, boosting engine power output by 30% to 100% without increasing the physical bore, stroke, or engine weight. It is essential for aircraft engines to compensate for altitude power loss.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the key functional difference between a 'Supercharger' and a 'Turbocharger' in internal combustion engines?

options.A: A supercharger is driven by exhaust gases, while a turbocharger is driven mechanically by a belt from the crankshaft
options.B: A supercharger compressor is mechanically driven by the engine crankshaft (drawing parasitic engine power), while a turbocharger compressor is driven by an exhaust gas turbine utilizing waste exhaust enthalpy without parasitic mechanical shaft load
options.C: A turbocharger operates only with pure steam
options.D: A supercharger cannot be used on diesel engines

explanation: A mechanical Supercharger is geared or belt-driven directly from the engine crankshaft; although it delivers instant boost without lag, it consumes substantial engine power (parasitic shaft work), reducing net brake thermal efficiency. A Turbocharger consists of a centrifugal compressor paired on a common shaft with a radial inflow turbine. The turbine is spun entirely by the high-pressure, high-temperature exhaust gas blowdown that would otherwise be wasted to the atmosphere, recovering thermal energy and providing superior overall engine efficiency.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: Why is an 'Aftercooler' (Intercooler) virtually always incorporated between the turbocharger compressor and the engine intake manifold?

options.A: To condense liquid water into the intake manifold
options.B: Compressing air heats it up significantly, reducing its density; cooling the compressed air in an intercooler increases its charge density (allowing more air mass into cylinders) and lowers combustion temperatures, preventing knock in petrol engines and reducing thermal stress
options.C: To increase the velocity of incoming air to sonic speed
options.D: To filter unburned fuel droplets out of the intake air

explanation: According to gas laws, adiabatic compression in a turbocharger heats intake air up to 120-180 deg C, causing thermal expansion that severely offsets density gains. Passing this hot boost air through an air-to-air or air-to-water Intercooler cools the air back toward ambient temperature. This significantly increases charge density (more oxygen molecules per unit volume) and suppresses pre-ignition/detonation in petrol engines while reducing peak flame temperatures that cause NOx emissions in diesel engines.

subject: THERMAL ENGINEERING
question: What is the operational function of an Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) system in internal combustion engines, and what pollutant does it primarily reduce?

options.A: It recirculates carbon monoxide into the crankcase to improve fuel economy
